passage: "Listen to that," said Nani, laughing. "Wasim thumps his bowl, and now Arnab thumps his." "Watch, he waits for Wasim first," said Mummy, setting down the dal. The two boys grinned at each other. Wasim clapped. Arnab clapped a moment later, not knowing why. "Now Wasim shakes his head at the beans." "And Arnab shakes his head too, with a full mouth!" The baby in Nani's lap only chewed a rusk and watched.

qa.q: What did Arnab do after Wasim thumped his bowl?
qa.a: Arnab thumped his own bowl, and later clapped after Wasim clapped.

qa.q: What does Arnab's waiting for Wasim before each action suggest about why Arnab does it?
qa.a: It suggests Arnab is simply copying Wasim, with no idea of rules; Arnab seems happy and delighted to do whatever Wasim does, as the grin between the two boys shows.

qa.q: How could a caregiver make use of this copying in a gentle way?
qa.a: A caregiver could show a calm action, such as patting the table softly or eating a bean, and let the toddlers copy that, since imitation is how they learn.

qa.q: How might the baby in Nani's lap be experiencing the banging and clapping?
qa.a: The baby chews a rusk and watches, so the noise is something to look at rather than something to join yet.

grounding: A toddler imitates the child beside them, banging and clapping only because the other did, with no notion of rules.

passage: Toddler room note, Tuesday. At snack Lakshmi pushed her banana slices away and screwed up her face. Trisha, who had eaten banana happily all week, looked across, pushed her own plate away and made the same face. Then Imran did it too. Only Deepa kept eating, without looking up. None of them seemed to be objecting to the fruit itself. I put the banana back without comment and will offer it again tomorrow. — Anita, toddler room carer

qa.q: Who kept eating banana while the others pushed their plates away?
qa.a: Deepa kept eating, without looking up.

qa.q: Why did Trisha push away banana after eating it happily all week?
qa.a: Trisha was probably not unhappy with the banana at all; watching Lakshmi, Trisha seems curious and keen to copy the face and gesture, since nothing about the fruit had changed.

qa.q: What did Anita choose to do about the refused banana, and why is that a sensible choice?
qa.a: Anita put the banana back without comment and planned to offer it again tomorrow, which avoids making the refusal a battle for children who are only imitating.

qa.q: What might snack time be like for Deepa, who kept eating while three others refused?
qa.a: Deepa may be the child least affected by the others; eating without looking up suggests Deepa is absorbed in the food rather than in what the group does.

grounding: Toddlers refuse a food because the child beside them does, showing pure imitation with no idea of approval.

passage: Lunch at the colony daycare was dal-rice. Hrithik sat between Kalyani and a smaller boy, Bittu. Kalyani lifted her steel spoon and banged it on her tray. Bang, bang, bang. Hrithik stared at her, then grabbed his own spoon and banged too, laughing. Bittu joined a second later. The helper didi tapped a slow beat with them, then offered each child a bite. The noise stopped.

qa.q: What did Kalyani bang on her tray?
qa.a: Kalyani banged her steel spoon on her tray.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling as he banged his spoon?
qa.a: He looked delighted and excited; he stared at Kalyani first and then laughed while copying her.

qa.q: How did the helper calm the banging without scolding?
qa.a: The helper joined the beat for a moment, then put the plate down and offered each child a bite, so the game ended gently.

qa.q: How might Bittu have experienced the banging game?
qa.a: Bittu probably found it fun and simply followed the older two; he joined a second later without any idea of a rule.

grounding: Shows a toddler copying the spoon-banging of the child beside him, pure imitation with no sense of rules or approval.

passage:
“Look, Anirban has pushed his bowl away,” said Farida's mother.
“No!” said Anirban, shaking his head at the mashed pumpkin.
Farida looked at him, then at her own bowl. “No!” she copied, and shoved it too.
“She ate pumpkin yesterday,” laughed Anirban's father. “She's copying him.”
“Shall we try?” Farida's mother took a spoonful herself. “Mmm. Yummy.”
Anirban leaned in and opened his mouth. Farida opened hers straight after.
“Copycats,” his father said.

qa.q: What food did Anirban push away?
qa.a: He pushed away his bowl of mashed pumpkin.

qa.q: Why did Farida shove her bowl away?
qa.a: She was not upset about the pumpkin; she felt curious and eager to do what Anirban did, since she had eaten it happily yesterday.

qa.q: What worked to get both toddlers eating again?
qa.a: Farida's mother ate a spoonful herself and made it look tasty, giving the toddlers something new to copy instead of arguing.

qa.q: How does Anirban's father see the moment?
qa.a: He finds it funny and sweet rather than naughty; he calls them copycats and wipes both chins.

grounding: Shows a toddler refusing a food only because the child beside her refuses it, pure imitation without rules.

passage:
Playgroup note, Thursday.
During the rain rhyme, Ganga clapped at the end. Pranav watched her hands, not mine, and clapped too, a beat late and proud of himself. When Ganga got up and wandered to the window, Pranav followed at once, and so did little Moti. I carried the drum over and started the rhyme again there. All three clapped. Next week I will seat Pranav beside children who are joining in.

qa.q: Where did Ganga wander during the rhyme?
qa.a: Ganga got up and wandered to the window.

qa.q: How did Pranav seem to feel when he clapped?
qa.a: He seemed proud and happy; he watched Ganga's hands rather than the teacher's and clapped a beat after her.

qa.q: Why was moving the drum to the window a sensible choice?
qa.a: It used the toddlers' copying instead of fighting it, so the rhyme carried on where they were and all three joined in.

qa.q: What might Moti's part show about the group?
qa.a: Moti seems to follow whoever moves first, just like Pranav, so one child's action spreads through the little group.

grounding: Shows a toddler clapping and wandering because the child beside him does, imitation that is the root of later fitting in.

passage: At the village anganwadi, three toddlers sat in a row on the mat with their steel plates. Urmila, the oldest, banged her spoon on her plate. Clang! Little Sabina watched, then banged hers too, grinning. Soon the boy beside her was banging as well. When Urmila pushed away her bitter gourd, Sabina pushed hers away too, though she had eaten it happily the day before. The anganwadi didi laughed and gave each of them a piece of banana.

qa.q: What did Urmila bang on her plate?
qa.a: Her spoon.

qa.q: Why did Sabina push away her bitter gourd?
qa.a: Sabina was simply copying Urmila, feeling playful and delighted by the game, not disliking the food, since she had eaten it happily the day before.

qa.q: What could the anganwadi didi try next time with the bitter gourd?
qa.a: Eat a piece cheerfully herself, or seat Sabina beside a child who is eating it, since the toddlers copy what they see.

qa.q: How might the anganwadi didi see the banging?
qa.a: Probably amused, seeing it as a playful copying game spreading down the row.

grounding: Toddlers copy each other's spoon-banging and food refusal as pure imitation, without any sense of rules.
